name: Termanu
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

new_statements.quote: § 4. Het accent, dat in het Rottineesch duidelijk hoorbaar is, valt bij een tweelettergrepig stamwoord of bij de afleidingen daarvan, als ook op de drielettergrepige, welke voor de tegenwoordige taal als stamwoord gelden, (bijv. bolau, spin), steeds op de vóór-laatste lettergreep. Op de laatste lettergreep valt de klemtoon bij alle afleidingen van één-lettergrepige stamwoorden, [...] of bij zulke samenstellingen, waarvan een één-lettergrepig woord het laatste lid uitmaakt [...] Tevens is echter in 't oog te houden, dat de vocaal hierbij altijd gerekt is [...] [p. 6:] Verspringing van den klemtoon komt in het Rottineesch in de tegenwoordige taal niet voor.
new_statements.translation: Sec. 4. The accent, which is clearly audible in Rotinese, falls in a disyllabic stem word or in its derivatives, as also in the trisyllabic words that count as stems for the present-day language (e.g. bolau 'spider'), always on the penultimate syllable. The stress falls on the last syllable in all derivatives of monosyllabic stems [...] or in such compounds of which a monosyllabic word forms the last member [...] It must also be kept in mind that the vowel is then always lengthened [...] [p. 6:] Shifting of the stress does not occur in present-day Rotinese.
new_statements.citation: Jonker, J. C. G. 1915. Rottineesche Spraakkunst. Leiden: E. J. Brill.
new_statements.locator: Eerste Deel 'Klanken, Klemtoon, Schrift', sec. 4 'De Klemtoon', printed pp. 5-6 (Delpher scan pp. 33-34)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (symlink to, 714-pp Delpher scan) and its scanned. The quoted sec. 4 passage is at scanned line 347 (=== SCANPAGE 33 ===) and 'Verspringing van den klemtoon komt in het Rottineesch in de tegenwoordige taal niet voor. Eigenlijke woord-vormende suffixen ontbreken en de pronominale aanhechtsels, enz., hebben hier deze werking niet.' at line 357 (SCANPAGE 34). I rendered scan p. 33 (page render, 60 dpi) and read the image: header 'ROTTINEESCHE SPRAAKKUNST. 5', and the printed text of sec. 4 matches the reader's quote word for word ('Het accent, dat in het Rottineesch duidelijk hoorbaar is, valt bij een tweelettergrepig stamwoord of bij de afleidingen daarvan, als ook op de drielett…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word accent is fixed on the penultimate syllable of stems (di- and trisyllabic) and their derivatives. Apparent final accent occurs only when the last member is a monosyllabic root (derivative or compound), whose vowel is always long, plus a few lexicalised words (palák 'old', kaifú, kelumèk); Edwards 2021 reanalyses these as final double vowels /VV/, making the rule 'stress the penultimate vowel' exceptionless. Accent never shifts: there are no true word-forming suffixes and pronominal attachments do not attract or move it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jonker sec. 4 (p. 5): words of more than three syllables (or trisyllables with final accent), whether stems or compounds, have a double accent - the strongest on the penult (or final), a weaker one on the fourth (or third) syllable from the end (luü-eik: secondary on lu; kelumèk: on ke); a monosyllabic first member of a compound keeps relative length under the secondary accent; still-living prefixes (and be, beke) never take secondary accent (p. 6). Edwards 2021:12, 35: 'Secondary stress is assigned to every second syllable to the left.'
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in derivatives of monosyllabic roots and compounds ending in a monosyllabic root (peta-bá, lima-lè), always with a lengthened vowel; a few di-/trisyllabic words now felt as roots with final accent (palák, kaifú, kaifòk, kelumèk); reduplicated final portions stay a unit so the secondary accent sits further from the main accent (kaki-uüle, kai-lií); prefixes felt as such never bear secondary accent (napadeik, nangatuk accented only on de, tuk); in loans an epenthetic vowel can move the accent onto the new penult (holomata < hormat, p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of stems and derived/compound words in the Termanu dialect; sec. 2 states the long-accented/short-unaccented vowel pattern holds for words in isolation or in pausa as well as in connected speech and composition; accent does not shift when short pronominal forms are attached (sec. 4 p. 6 and the Aanm. in the pronoun chapter). Jonker adds the caveat (p. 6 Aanm.) that the topic can only be treated 'in general', by ear.
new_statements.identity_note: Jonker 1915 is a grammar of 'Rottineesch' that by its own Inleiding 'behandelt in hoofdzaak den tongval van Termanoe' (treats chiefly the Termanu/Pada dialect, = Glottolog term1237), with other Rote dialects discussed alongside; the accent rule in sec. 4 is stated for Rotinese generally with Termanu forms. Edwards 2021 sec. 1.4.1.2 states the stress facts explicitly 'in Termanu'; his sec. 2.4.1 restates them for all Rote languages.

sources.locator: Eerste Deel 'Klanken, Klemtoon, Schrift', sec. 4 'De Klemtoon', printed pp. 5-6 (Delpher scan pp. 33-34)
sources.note: Part I 'Klanken, Klemtoon, Schrift', sec. 4 (pp. 5-6): accent clearly audible; always on the penultimate syllable of disyllabic stems and their derivatives and of trisyllables now counting as stems; on the final syllable only in derivatives of monosyllabic roots / compounds whose last member is a monosyllabic root (vowel then always lengthened) and a few lexicalised words (palák, kaifú, kelumèk); words of 4+ syllables carry a weaker secondary accent on the 4th/3rd syllable from the end; living prefixes never bear secondary accent; 'Verspringing van den klemtoon komt... niet voor' - no stress…

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2021. Rote-Meto Comparative Dictionary. Canberra: ANU Press (Asia-Pacific Linguistics).
sources.note: Sec. 1.4.1.2 (pp. 11-12), summarising Termanu vowel phonology: 'Stress is penultimate. Secondary stress is assigned to every second syllable to the left.' and 'Given that stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word, a double vowel will always contain a vowel that is the locus of stress'; Jonker's final-accented forms (nadá, na-tafú) reanalysed as final double vowels /aa/, /uu/. Sec. 2.4.1 (p. 35), Rote languages generally: 'Stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word with secondary stress assigned to every second syllable to the left.'
